title: 2026-03-30 technical deep dive: Multi-region routing & failover

Agreed next steps: Redwood to share routing policy draft, region capacity spreadsheet, and run a failover DR test window.

transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-03-30 15:00 UTC | Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Avery Chen (Redwood AE), Marcus Lee (Redwood SE), Elena Park (Redwood Solutions), Sasha Martinez (CTO - Atlas Financial), Devon Brooks (Platform Eng), Priya Nair (SRE), Liam O'Connor (Security)

[00:00] Avery Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. We're planning a focused deep dive on multi-region routing and failover for Atlas. Marcus and Elena from our engineering side will lead the technical parts. Quick quick intro round?
[00:12] Sasha Martinez: Sasha here, CTO at Atlas. We're preparing for an upcoming migration of transaction enrichment to Redwood and need high availability across NA and EU with DR in APAC.
[00:22] Devon Brooks: Devon, I run platform ops, mainly interested in routing, capacity, and how KV cache behavior will affect warm starts.
[00:28] Priya Nair: Priya, SRE, owning runbooks and incident playbooks. Key for us: predictable RTO and RPO and controlled failover.
[00:36] Liam O'Connor: Liam from security, we'll be checking VPC peering and KMS/HSM considerations.
[00:42] Marcus Lee: Great. Quick agenda: routing policy models, regional capacity and model variants, cache considerations (KV prefix caching), batching and latency tradeoffs, quantization effects, VPC/on-prem constraints, and an outline DR playbook.

[02:10] Marcus Lee: To start, we recommend a policy-driven router — basically, metadata + SLOs determine route. E.g., route by region affinity first, then by SLA tier, then by cost. If region capacity under threshold, automatically failover to the next compatible region.
[02:28] Sasha Martinez: Compatible region meaning same model/quantization profile? We can't afford large QA regressions across regions.
[02:36] Marcus Lee: Exactly. We maintain model variants keyed by two axes: architecture and quantization profile. The router only fails over to a variant that matches a compatibility matrix. For example, if you're on gpt-like-2 q4_0, we won't fail to a q2 variant unless you accept quality degradation.
[03:05] Elena Park: Small note: we also support functionally equivalent models when exact variant isn't available. Those are labeled as "compatibility fallback" and flagged in response metadata so you can track which responses came from fallbacks.

[04:00] Devon Brooks: How do you keep KV cache warm when traffic cross-regions? Our sessions are latency sensitive, 100-150ms p95. Cold KV loads on failover would spike latencies.
[04:15] Marcus Lee: Great question. Two approaches: proactive prefix replication and on-demand warmed transfer. Proactive replication means we asynchronously replicate hot KV prefixes to secondary regions based on access frequency. That reduces warm-up but increases cross-region egress and storage costs.
[04:34] Sasha Martinez: Can we set thresholds? Like only replicate prefixes with >X qps or >Y tokens per minute?
[04:40] Marcus Lee: Yes. The router emits metrics and we have heuristics: any prefix with >50 qps or that contributes >20% of your token volume can be hot-replicated. These numbers are tunable.
[05:02] Priya Nair: On-demand warm transfer — what's the window? We need an estimate of how long a cold call will add to latency.
[05:10] Marcus Lee: On-demand transfer will add the time to rebuild the KV from origin, which for long context windows can be 200-400ms for large prefixes. If you accept a short degradation we can tier it: first serve with truncated KV then asynchronously fill in the rest and subsequent calls are fast.

[06:12] Sasha Martinez: Okay, this is useful. Next: routing decision latency. We don't want the router to add 20-30ms on every request.
[06:20] Marcus Lee: Our routing layer is optimized — policy evaluation happens in sub-ms in the common path via precomputed rule tables, but there's a small hop for health checks. In practice it's 2-6ms median. For extreme low-latency workloads we can inline routing decisions at the edge using a signed policy blob so that the request hits the chosen region directly.
[06:46] Devon Brooks: What about batching? We sometimes need to aggregate many small requests to stay cost-effective. How do you manage batching during partial failovers?
[06:56] Elena Park: Batching is managed per region node pool. If a region is partially degraded and you still route some traffic there, batching windows will adapt downward to keep p95 in range. When we're failing traffic out, we prefer to keep batching parameters conservative in the receiving region to avoid large latency spikes.

[08:10] Priya Nair: Quantization: our legal team wants quantized models for cost reasons. Does switching quantization affect latency predictably across hardware?
[08:20] Marcus Lee: Yes and it's hardware-dependent. On some GPUs, lower-bit quantization reduces token compute and latency. On others, it increases kernel fragmentation and slightly increases latency for short sequences. We publish performance profiles per model/quantization/hardware. The router uses those profiles to choose the low-cost region that meets latency SLOs.

[09:40] Sasha Martinez: For regulatory reasons we need EU data residency for EU users. Can routing be scoped by residency tags?
[09:48] Marcus Lee: Absolutely. We support routing by residency — it's the top rule. Requests with EU residency tags are pinned to EU regions except when explicit failover is allowed by policy. In that case, failover requires a documented exception and is logged/audited.

[11:10] Liam O'Connor: VPC peering and traffic egress — if we fail over to a region where we don't have direct VPC peering, what's the network model?
[11:20] Marcus Lee: Two primary patterns: we can bring up a temporary secure tunnel (mTLS + IP allowlist) to a Redwood-managed VPC in the failover region, or you can set up cross-region VPC peering in advance. Temporary tunnels are quicker but add a small hop and must be approved by security.
[11:44] Liam O'Connor: HSM/KMS keys — do you support key replication?
[11:49] Elena Park: We do not replicate customer-managed keys across regions by default; instead we integrate with your KMS in each region. For private deployments we can support import/export under strict controls. Replicating keys has legal implications; usually customers provision equivalent keys in each region and we handle key references.

[13:10] Devon Brooks: Walk us through a typical failover playbook — what's the sequence?
[13:18] Marcus Lee: High-level sequence: detection -> ring-down (throttle non-critical traffic) -> partial failover (route lower priority traffic first) -> full failover (if needed) -> KV warm-up & validation -> rollback if errors. We recommend a staged failover: first route canary traffic (1-5%) to target region, validate correctness and latency, then increase to 25% then 100%.
[13:50] Priya Nair: How do we validate correctness? We need semantic checks beyond latency, e.g., answer quality and hallucination rates.
[13:58] Marcus Lee: Redwood supports synthetic prompt sets and eval harnesses that can be run during canaries. You can attach a small eval set that checks for key invariants (accuracy, safety, hallucination). The router flags responses served during canary with head_metadata so they're easy to slice in logs.

[15:30] Sasha Martinez: What about partial outages — e.g., a single AZ or a subset of nodes in region degraded. Do you failover at node granularity?
[15:38] Elena Park: We do health-aware routing at node and pool granularity. For AZ flaps we drain and fail partial traffic while keeping warm cache tiers as possible. If it's a localized issue we can avoid full region failover.

[17:00] Devon Brooks: Testing — we want to run a DR failover test in the non-prod account first, then a planned failover in prod. What's the recommended test plan and metrics?
[17:08] Marcus Lee: Proposed plan: non-prod run-through: 1) baseline capture (qps, p95, p99, token cost), 2) canary failover to region B (5%) run 30m, run eval set, capture regressions, 3) increase to 25% 30m, 4) full 100% for 15m then rollback. Metrics: p95/p99 latency, error rate, cost delta, KV warm-up time, eval pass rate. For prod plan add a business-owner approval gate and run during low-traffic window.

[18:56] Priya Nair: Are there tooling hooks for automation? We want the failover to be reproducible in our pipeline.
[19:03] Elena Park: Yes — everything is exposed via API and IaC. We can supply Terraform modules to define routing policies, and playbooks can be triggered via API for automated failovers. We also support webhook callbacks on state transitions.

[20:30] Sasha Martinez: Can you show an example policy DSL?
[20:34] Marcus Lee: (screen share described) The policy DSL is rule-based, e.g.,
- rule: residency == EU -> route EU pool
- rule: SLO==gold AND p95_target<=150ms -> prefer region with profile matching p95
- fallback: allow_compatibility_fallback=false

[21:20] Devon Brooks: A practical concern — how do we monitor when failover increases egress/costs? We need thresholds that auto-notify finance.
[21:28] Marcus Lee: Router emits cost estimates per route and a failover cost delta. You can set budget thresholds to auto-alert. We also provide token-level cost breakdowns and tagging so you can attribute to services.

[23:05] Liam O'Connor: Audit logs — we need complete tamper-evident records for failover decisions.
[23:12] Elena Park: We stream audit logs to your SIEM and support signed audit events. We can integrate with your Cloud Audit Logging. For Private deployments we can push to your on-prem Splunk.

[24:45] Sasha Martinez: Any known gotchas?
[24:49] Marcus Lee: A few: 1) cold KV warmup is the biggest surprise — plan replication for heavy prefixes; 2) model compatibility mismatches during fallback can change semantics; 3) VPC peering differences can add latency and DNS nuances.

[26:00] Devon Brooks: About model compatibility — can we run A/B test to quantify semantic drift between variants?
[26:10] Marcus Lee: Yes, we recommend an A/B evaluation: route 10% to variant B with logging and run the eval harness. We provide side-by-side scoring for your prompt set.

[28:00] Priya Nair: For on-prem/private deployments, can we do cross-site replication of KV?
[28:08] Elena Park: For private installs, we support tenant-aware replication across your sites via async replication. It's customer-managed but we provide the replication controller. There are tradeoffs: replication lag and eventual consistency must be accounted for in the runbook.

[29:30] Sasha Martinez: Latency budgets again — what are typical numbers on Redwood for the combination of routing + model infer for a 1k token request in NA?
[29:40] Marcus Lee: On a balanced setup with q4_0 on A100-ish hardware, median routing+infer is ~120ms for 1k tokens with batching enabled, p95 around 210-260ms depending on batch pressure. For shortest-latency we can do streaming configs that hit ~80-100ms median but cost more.

[31:20] Devon Brooks: Can you attach the per-model perf profiles to the routing engine so it picks based on actual observed p95 rather than the published table?
[31:30] Marcus Lee: Yes — router can use live telemetry to adapt decisions. There's an adaptive mode where we bias toward regions with lower recent p95. It smooths over short variance windows to avoid flapping.

[33:10] Elena Park: A short note about expiry and stale cache: when we failover we tag KV entries with origin region and TTLs. If the origin updates, we invalidate stale entries via a version vector; worst-case you'll get a brief inconsistency window.

[34:50] Sasha Martinez: What about long-tail failures — if APAC has a major outage, do we support manual policy overrides to force global fallback?
[34:58] Marcus Lee: Yes, you can set manual global overrides, and those are recorded in the audit log and require an approver if you want. We also have a scheduled maintenance mode.

[36:20] Priya Nair: Can Redwood's suggestions for which prefixes to replicate be exported so we can run internal ROI calculations?
[36:26] Marcus Lee: We'll include a heatmap CSV with estimated cross-region egress and cost delta per prefix. That should help your finance and infra decide thresholds.

[37:50] Sasha Martinez: Anything about encryption in transit across regions?
[37:55] Elena Park: All intra-region and inter-region traffic is encrypted via TLS 1.3 and mutual auth for VPC peering/tunnels. We support customer mTLS certs for critical links.

[39:00] Devon Brooks: Proposed timeline: we want a non-prod DR test by Apr 13 and a prod window late April. Can Redwood support runbooks and someone on-call during tests?
[39:10] Avery Chen: Yes, we can provide an SE-run DR session and be on-call during your test windows. We'll also provide the Terraform modules and the routing policy examples.

[40:05] Marcus Lee: I'll follow up with the policy DSL examples, compatibility matrix for your pinned models, and a capacity spreadsheet. Expect that by 2026-04-02.

[40:20] Sasha Martinez: Great. A couple of quick clarifying questions: if we allow cross-region failover for EU users under exceptions, is there an automated GDPR checklist?
[40:30] Liam O'Connor: I'll need to sign off on any exception but want automation — like a checkbox and a record of legal consent.
[40:36] Marcus Lee: We can add an exception object in the policy DSL that requires a signed consent artifact before auto-failover to non-residency regions. That artifact is stored and referenced in audit logs.

[42:00] Devon Brooks: One more — can we limit failover to model-serving only and keep sensitive telemetry in-region?
[42:08] Elena Park: Yes, you can route inference to other regions while telemetry/PII logs remain in residency region by default. That separation is configurable.

[43:10] Priya Nair: Final recap and owners?
[43:16] Avery Chen: Recap: Redwood to share policy draft, capacity spreadsheet, and canary failover plan (Marcus/Elena). Atlas to provide traffic patterns and owners for approvals (Sasha/Devon/Priya). Set DR test in non-prod week of Apr 13. SE on-call during tests.
[43:36] Sasha Martinez: Sounds good. Thanks everyone.
[43:40] Avery Chen: Thanks, we'll follow up.

[44:00] (end)

Notes about transcript quality: auto-transcribed with a few mis-hearings (e.g., "KV" sometimes transcribed as "K V", some product names simplified). References: shared doc link: https://redwood.example.com/routing-policy/atlas-draft (Redwood routing draft), capacity spreadsheet: https://redwood.example.com/spreadsheets/atlas-capacity (view-only), DR runbook template: https://docs.redwood.com/runbooks/dr-template.pdf
